item.title: Medical Radioisotopes: Clinical Demand, Production Physics, and Untapped Pathways
item.description: arXiv:2611.08727v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Over 40 radioisotopes are currently in use or under development across virtually all fields of modern medicine. Their availability relies on a complex interplay of nuclear physics, radiochemistry, and nuclear medicine. This review provides an isotope-by-isotope map of medically important radioisotopes from the perspective of these disparate yet complementary fields. We address the landscape grouped into three tiers: the established clinical core, including, familiar workhorses such as Tc-99m, F-18, Lu-177; an under-leveraged middle tier including Re-186, Re-188, and Sm-153, and the emerging frontier, radioisotopes with demonstrated but underutilised clinical promise such as Ac-225, At-211, Cu-67, and Sc-47. We discuss the properties of these radioisotopes with respect to clinical applications and their production pathways, as well as the associated nuclear and radiochemical challenges. We synthesise these disparate perspectives to identify situations in which alleviating production-side bottlenecks may improve access and patient outcomes.
item.dc:creator: Jarrett Moon, Claire Huchthausen, Jose R Alonso, Shadi A Esfahani, Faraz Farhadi, David McClain, Hamid Sabet, Pedram Heidari, Janet M Conrad, Daniel Winklehner

item.title: Medical Radioisotopes: Supply-chain Resilience, Distributed Production, and Access
item.description: arXiv:2611.08734v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Over 50 million diagnostic procedures involving medical radioisotopes are performed per year and the number of therapeutic and theranostic agents continues to climb. Yet, the global supply chain is far from stable and many regions are underserved. This is the second of a Series of two review papers providing a comprehensive overview of the landscape of medically relevant radioisotopes. This paper focuses on the supply chain. It presents a critical overview of the 2025-2026 status quo, case studies of acute stressors and disruptions they caused, and methods in place to secure a stable supply. A literature-based analysis is paired with expert interviews. We argue that the ageing fleet of nuclear reactors currently used for the centralised production of many isotopes should be complemented by regional accelerator-based centres, alleviating single-point failures and cross-border logistics complications, and increasing access to short-lived isotopes in harder-to-reach regions and low- and middle-income countries.
item.dc:creator: David McClain, Daniel Winklehner, Faraz Farhadi, Jose R Alonso, Shadi A Esfahani, Claire Huchthausen, Jarrett Moon, Hamid Sabet, Pedram Heidari, Janet M Conrad

item.title: Dual-energy cardiac DSA imaging using a dual-layer flat-panel detector: in vivo validation study
item.description: arXiv:2611.08820v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Background: The temporal misregistration in conventional X-ray digital subtraction angiography (DSA) remains a key challenge for its practical application in cardiac catheterization, leading to incomplete separation of cardiac vessels from background anatomical structures. Purpose: In this study, the X-ray spectral information is unveiled for DSA imaging to generate better visualization of cardiac vessels with negligible anatomical background. Methods: A dedicated dual-energy DSA imaging model is proposed based on the subtraction residuals between pre-contrast and post-contrast spectral projections, enabling accurate material decomposition without requiring precise scatter correction. Specifically, a dual-layer flat-panel detector (DL-FPD) is assumed to acquire the needed temporally registered low-energy and high-energy projections. Moreover, a penalized likelihood material decomposition algorithm is proposed to enhance the material decomposition performance. To validate, in vivo swine experiments were conducted for the first time on a clinical DSA system equipped with a DL-FPD. Results: Monte Carlo simulation results demonstrated that the impact of scatter on the subtraction residuals can be reduced by more than 80%, substantially improving material decomposition accuracy. Compared with analytical material decomposition, the penalized-likelihood material decomposition algorithm significantly improves image contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), enabling the visualization of small vessels and even the myocardial blush effect. Furthermore, compared with conventional dual-energy subtraction, the penalized-likelihood approach provides more quantitative material maps with fewer overlapping anatomical background artifacts. Conclusion: This preliminary study verifies that dual-energy DSA imaging method is able to generate high-quality cardiovascular imaging results.
item.dc:creator: Yuhang Tan, Jiongtao Zhu, Xin Zhang, Haodi Wu, Xiao Xuan, Mang Feng, Mingzhi Cui, Hairong Zheng, Dong Liang, Yongshuai Ge

item.title: Smart Spectral Doppler Ultrasound Imaging using Motion Tracking based on Wide-beam transmission and Neural Networks: Preliminary Results
item.description: arXiv:2611.09002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ultrasound spectral Doppler imaging provides quantitative blood flow information for vascular diagnosis, but its accuracy is limited by the one-dimensional (1D) sample volume (SV). Motion from respiration, patient movement, and probe manipulation can move the target vessel out of the SV, causing spectral broadening, signal reduction, or loss of the spectrum. A two-dimensional (2D) SV can address this, but sequential focused-beam transmission reduces the pulse-repetition frequency (PRF), and plane-wave transmission lowers the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). In this study, we propose a wide-beam transmission method that acquires a 2D SV from a single transmit event while preserving the PRF. A Hamming network, which requires no prior training, tracks axial and lateral motion within the 2D SV and updates the position of an adaptive 1D SV for each frame. Field II simulations showed that the wide-beam transmission had a spectral SNR comparable to that of focused-beam transmission and approximately 10 dB higher than that of plane-wave transmission. The motion tracking correctly detected the target position in over 93% of frames for vessel radii greater than 1 mm, and in 100% of frames for radii greater than 2 mm. In vivo studies of a carotid artery (linear array) and a hepatic vein (convex array) showed that the proposed method recovered obscured spectra and increased the spectral SNR by 9.3 dB and 4.5 dB, respectively. These results demonstrate that the proposed wide-beam transmission with Hamming network-based tracking can improve the accuracy of spectral Doppler imaging under tissue motion. Moreover, we anticipate that the proposed approach can be implemented in real-time due to its single transmission and simple two-layer architecture with low computational complexity.
item.dc:creator: Jihye Baek, Allison Lee, Jinbum Kang, Yangmo Yoo

item.title: SmartBloch-Agent: An Agentic Framework for Automated MRI Sequence Design and Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.09413v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) pulse sequences organize radiofrequency excitation, gradient encoding, and signal acquisition, determining magnetization evolution and image formation. Sequence research requires translating imaging objectives into executable protocols meeting physical and acquisition constraints, refined via physical simulation, signal reconstruction, and scientific evaluation. Sequence construction, physical verification, parameter search, and assessment involve many tools and manual decisions, limiting automation from objective to verifiable sequence. We develop SmartBloch-Agent, an integrated framework for automated MRI sequence design and optimization. Given objectives and scientific constraints in natural language, an AI agent interprets goals, plans tasks, orchestrates tools, and makes feedback-informed decisions, drawing on a construction module and optimizers for structural design and parameter search. Our GPU-accelerated SmartBloch engine supplies physical computation for both stages, so the framework configures, per sequence and objective, event validation, Full-Bloch magnetization evolution, signal acquisition, image reconstruction, and scientific evaluation, and closes the loop without external MRI simulators. Results return to the agent to guide sequence revision, parameter optimization, and candidate selection, and the design files carry simulation, reconstruction, and evaluation evidence, forming an output package for a real-scanner workflow. Experiments show the framework automatically designs and optimizes MRI sequences for varied objectives and constraints, refines candidates with physical feedback, and improves several parameter-estimation metrics and downstream quantitative reconstruction. SmartBloch-Agent unifies objectives, design, physical execution, and evaluation into a continuous workflow for end-to-end automation of MRI sequence research.
item.dc:creator: Jiakai Yang, Haoye Zheng, Yixiao Yue, Qinqin Yang, Zhong Chen, Shuhui Cai, Congbo Cai
